annotations.text:
Five ways to set the same three lines of Jackson's list.

The masthead and the foot are IDENTICAL in all six — only the table changes, so the comparison is fair. Every direction fixes the two faults: the section title is a different RANK from a product name, and packing spells its noun (20 Boxes/Ctn, not 20/Ctn).

Far left is what ships today, for comparison.

A · LEDGER — rank by POSITION. The section label leaves the product column and sits in a left gutter, so it can never be read as a line item. Most formal; most like a trade document. Costs 100px of width.
B · REVERSED BAND — rank by GROUND. White type on a dark bar cannot be mistaken for a product at any weight. Strongest separation, boldest look; the bars eat vertical space on a long list.
C · PRICE FIRST — the figure is the headline, the name sits under it. Best at a WhatsApp thumbnail and at arm's length in the yard. Least like a conventional price list.
D · CARDS — each line is its own object on a tinted ground; the section is a quiet label above the stack. Friendliest, most modern. Fits fewer lines per picture than the others.
E · DOT LEADER — the oldest price-sheet device: the eye is walked from name to figure. Very familiar in this trade; the section is centred small caps, a different shape entirely from a product line.

The ruled grid, from your reference — and you were right that it is the price-list convention.

It also settles the rank argument for free: the section title sits OUTSIDE the box, in sentence case, so it cannot be read as a line of the table however it is set. No tracked capitals needed.

Five columns, one shape for every block: PRODUCT · PACKING · PER · PRICE · and a last column that changes with the block (YOU SAVE / YOU TAKE). The unit finally sits beside the price instead of at the far side of the row.

F · RULED GRID — closest to your reference. Every cell boxed, alternate rows banded, header row inside the rule with a heavier underline. The old price sits struck through under the new one, inside the money column where it belongs.

G · REVERSED HEAD — the same grid with a navy header row and no inner vertical rules. Reads lighter and more branded; the columns are held by alignment rather than by lines, which is a little weaker on a crowded sheet.

H · DENSE TRADE SHEET — every rule kept, banding dropped, rows tightened. Roughly twice as many lines fit on one picture, which matters once a real catalogue is behind this. Least friendly, most businesslike.
